3. Replication of Porretta et al. (2020)
3.1 Background and Motivation

17

We carried out a single change (web-based data collection) replication study of

18

Porretta et al. (2020)’s in-person VWP experiment.
decisions.location: Section 3.1 Background and Motivation, p. 10 (lines 734-743); References, p. 47 (lines 4627-4635)
decisions.reason: Both the shipped row and blind target 0 identify the same tested original study: Porretta, Buchanan, & Järvikivi (2020), 'When processing costs impact predictive processing: The case of foreign-accented speech and accent experience'. The authors explicitly state in the Abstract and Section 3.1 that they carried out a single-change (web-based) replication of Porretta et al. (2020)'s in-person visual world paradigm experiment.

decisions.quote:
Our replication results indicate that web-based eye-tracking can capture the same

6

predictive processing as in-person eye-tracking (e.g., Prystauka et al., 2023; Vos et al., 2022).

7

Our main models show that predictive sentence processing is modulated by restrictive and

8

non-restrictive verb type in line with Porretta et al. (2020) and that accented speech impedes

9

predictive processing but does not preclude it. Interestingly, our accent models did not find

10

evidence of accent-experience modulating predictive processing.
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind codings agree on 'mixed'. In Section 3.1 (lines 825-837), the authors specify that Porretta et al. (2020) investigated two research questions: (1) whether verb type modulates predictive processing in accented and unaccented speech, and (2) whether accent experience modulates prediction in accented speech. They re-test both via their Main Models (GLMM and GAMM) and Accent Models (GLMM and GAMM). In Section 4.3 and Section 5.1, their main models replicate Porretta et al. (2020)'s verb-type and accented-speech effects ('in line with Porretta et al. (2020)'), whereas their accent models 'did not find evidence of accent-experience modulating predictive processing' and are described as 'inconclusive with respect to the accent models' (discussing lower Chinese-accent exposure in the Prolific sample relative to Porretta et al.'s university sample, low power/Type-II error risk, and slider measurement error as reasons for 'the lack of evidence for an effect'). Addressing the blind coder's uncertainty note: the opening sentence of Section 5.1 about web-based eye-tracking capturing the same predictive processing as in-person eye-tracking is a methodological conclusion regarding RQ1 (which Section 3.1 notes is the only analysis that speaks to online eye-tracking quality), not an overall verdict that all tested findings of Porretta et al. (2020) replicated. Because the main-model comparison succeeded while the tested accent-experience effect did not replicate, 'mixed' is correct.

decisions.quote:
We demonstrate our

12

approach by carrying out a single change replication of an in-person eye-tracking study,

13

Porretta et al. (2020).
decisions.reason: The authors collected new web-based eye-tracking data from a fresh sample of 60 Prolific participants (49 analyzed after exclusions) using Porretta et al. (2020)'s recordings and design to re-test Porretta et al. (2020)'s findings. Both shipped and blind codings accurately classify the record as a 'replication'.
